extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; writers and students of literature and literary craft
extracted.subtask_description: Critical appraisal and guidance aimed at evaluating and understanding poetry, novels, and theatrical/history writing — focusing on matters of style, form, character, unity, and the relation of ideas to concrete life. Useful to critics, students, and creative writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical prejudice; favour the concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphysical prejudice for the 'Absolute,' the false intellectual conscience, and a 'fear of the actual' are detrimental to free and generous productivity in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic praises concrete engagement (historic institutions, lives of saints) over abstract isolation: failure of 'historic sense' leads to a glacial, rationalistic result. Writers should connect ideals with facts and venerable institutions to achieve fuller development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic sense / connection with institutions and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary mind should bring judgments into connection with the facts, the venerable institutions of the past, and the lives of the saints; lack of historic sense limits religious/intellectual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amiel is judged to have lacked the historic sense; the page argues that seeing Christianity as historic development would have matured his religious thought. Historical context should harmonize with spiritual/intellectual judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of life / plan
rubrics_metrics.description: "Welcome the unforeseen, but give to your life unity, and bring the unforeseen within the lines of your plan."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work (and life) should have unity; unexpected elements are valuable but should be assimilated into an overall plan of action, moral conception, or production to avoid fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of a 'book of thoughts' to being dipped into (quotability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book of 'thoughts' should be one that may be fairly dipped into and yield good quotable sayings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Journal is commended because it provides memorable aphorisms (several quoted). For the aphoristic form, density of quotable, self-contained sentences is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The skill of the translator affects reception: a good translation can help an author reach the best readers and extend the work's currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes how well Amiel's English translator has done her work, implying accuracy, tone, and style faithful to the original are relevant evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity vs. rightful obscurity (appropriateness of difficulty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity may be fault or appropriate difficulty; a writer dealing with 'high and hard questions' has a right to demand closeness of attention from readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning's alleged obscurity is defended: abstruse treatment is acceptable for the proper audience. The work should signal whether it expects sustained attention; unjustified obscurity is a fault, but complexity for complex subject-matter can be legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the arts of poetry (craft and finish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of poetic arts – finished skill, grace, music, lyric language — is a major positive quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symons praises Browning's finished art in short poems that render a single mood completely. Craft at line and phrase level (music, lyricism) is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume and variety as signs of genius (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of work and imaginative variety (becoming many persons) may indicate genius, even if uneven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning's large output and multitude of personae are cited as evidence of his endowment; unevenness can be tolerated in a prodigiously inventive author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the individual soul / development of a soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen subject-matter of important modern poetry/fiction is the individual, the inner life, and the development of a soul through incidents and acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning's work is praised for making each person 'an epitome of the universe' — interest lies in particular acts/episodes that test and reveal character. Writers should concentrate on concrete personal drama to reveal universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictorial and musical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that speaks the language of the painter and musician — vivid visual and musical imagination — is a distinctive strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Abt Vogler' as deep poem on music; 'A Toccata of Galuppi's' as rare rendering of musical impressions. Rich sensory metaphors and technical instincts of other arts can enrich verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with form (rhyme and metre) balanced with workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment in rhyme or metre is valuable but may be hazardous; intellectual depth can coexist with occasional apparent carelessness of workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning is described as an experimenter, sometimes 'hazardous'; later works show both profound intellectual depth and traces of carelessness. Authors should balance formal innovation with sufficient craft to avoid undermining the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of manner to material (dramatic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of presentation, style, and versification should suit the material; shifts in manner can mark evolution but may also disappoint those who idealize an earlier type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ring and the Book is seen as culmination of dramatic method; later changes in style (English/modern scenes vs medieval/foreign ones) are noted — changes are defensible but alter readers' ideal of an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evenness and consistency across a body of work
rubrics_metrics.description: A large and varied oeuvre may be uneven; consistency of excellence matters to one's conception of an 'ideal' author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though breadth is admired, the reviewer regrets certain later changes and unevenness; editors and readers will form an 'ideal' out of portions that best represent the author's strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/social resonance (humanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's capacity to 'listen to the music of humanity' and to render the soul-to-soul relation (moral sympathy) contributes to its lasting value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning is praised for social/listening qualities and the claim 'It lives, / If precious be the soul of man to man.' Moral and humanistic engagement strengthens longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiet evolution of character through circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel that traces the slow, realistic evolution of character in response to circumstances (Austen/George Sand model) is a legitimate and valuable method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robert Elsmere is commended as a 'chef d'oeuvre' of quiet evolution; such method requires length and patient composition to yield fully conceived characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level composition / building of a good sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient care in composition, especially at the sentence level, is an essential element of literary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs Ward's patient care in composition (building sentences) is singled out as a mark of cultivation; sentence craft supports unity and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of impression and smooth transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should ensure a final unity of impression and provide easy transition for the reader from one joint of interest to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer praises cohesion across many 'joints' in Mrs Ward's three volumes; authors should engineer transitions to maintain overall unity despite episodic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate length and pacing for method
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods (quiet, evolutionary character studies) require length; the reader's reward for patient reading must justify the lengthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes a 'lengthiness' required by the quiet method and that three volumes are fitting for full character development; choose form/length to match method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability, naturalness, and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability and nature — the plausibility of characters and events — are central to successful fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs Ward's instinct for probability and nature is praised; character actions and motives should feel natural, avoiding contrivance or schematic didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and authenticity in character portrayal (gendered strengths noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicately intuitive sympathy and authenticity in portraying characters (the reviewer notes Mrs Ward's greater success with women than men) are important virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should notice where an author achieves organic, sympathetic female portraits and where male characters feel composite or conventional; authenticity varies by character type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill with minor characters and ensemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to analyze and give life to minor characters enriches the texture of a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs Ward's analysis of minor characters (e.g., Richard Leyburn, Mrs Darcy) is highlighted as high cultivation; minor figures should feel vivid and contribute to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of setting/landscape into character and texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape and place should be more than background; they can shape character and become part of a book's texture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Westmorland scenery in Robert Elsmere acts spiritually and personally on characters (Wordsworthian influence). Evoked places should take hold on the reader as part of the experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational or Gothic elements to further ethical interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of sensation (ghosts, love-scenes) are acceptable when they advance the novel's ethical or psychological development rather than exist merely for shock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The haunted-girl episode and love-scenes in Robert Elsmere 'really further the development of the proper ethical interests of the book.' Avoid gratuitous sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic temper and plausibility in thematic development
rubrics_metrics.description: When a novel treats large philosophical or religious questions, the protagonist's intellectual journey should display a philosophic or scientific temper; abrupt or cavalier turns are a weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robert Elsmere's sudden decision and late perception are called a 'blot' on his pretensions; sustained, plausible inner development is required for credibility on serious themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of serious purpose with humour and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious thought benefits from moments of quiet humour which test and relieve the intensity of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs Ward's quiet humour is praised for testing sincerity of thought; tonal balance prevents heaviness and aids reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/illustrative apparatus enhances historical/collective works
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations, portraits, and topographical woodcuts add charm and information to historical or theatrical annals; selection and execution matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revised edition of Dr Doran with abundant illustrations is commended; however, portraits may not always explain the actors' power — images should illuminate text rather than merely decorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collector/critic's role as selector of the best rather than the dubious
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful introduction or guide should point readers to the best, the indisputable, rather than highlight dubious portions of an author's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr Symons' Introduction is praised for guiding readers to the strong parts of Browning's oeuvre and for providing biographical/contextual material; curatorial judgment aids new readers.
